claims.text: Grain-boundary density governs structural stability during high-temperature annealing of CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy nanoalloys.
Grain-boundary density governs chemical stability during high-temperature annealing of CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy nanoalloys.
Grain boundaries serve as rapid diffusion pathways in these nanoalloys.
Higher grain-boundary density delays phase separation by producing a more homogeneous diffusion profile.
Higher grain-boundary density delays grain coarsening up to a thermal threshold.
Inert gas condensation produces ultra-fine CoCrFeMnNi grains with high grain-boundary density.
Wet chemical synthesis produces larger CoCrFeMnNi grains than inert gas condensation.
Annealing at approximately 750°C under argon isolates diffusion-mediated coarsening and phase-evolution effects.
A high density of grain boundaries distributes diffusion flux more evenly and promotes compositional homogenization.
More uniform diffusion allows ultra-fine-grained samples to retain a metastable single-phase microstructure longer than samples with fewer grain boundaries.
Above a thermal threshold, high grain-boundary density can accelerate coarsening because diffusion becomes excessively activated.
Inert-gas-condensed nanoalloys will separate into phases more slowly during annealing than wet-chemically synthesized nanoalloys.
Inert-gas-condensed nanoalloys will retain a homogeneous metastable phase for longer during annealing than wet-chemically synthesized nanoalloys.
The as-synthesized samples are predominantly single phase.
The two as-synthesized sample sets differ only in grain size and grain-boundary density.
The predicted stabilization applies only while diffusion is activated along grain boundaries but before rapid coarsening occurs in both microstructures.
